pq_notes.A0: The authors argue that coastal space available for aquaculture is shaped by other interests, including fisheries, tourism, transport, conservation areas and military firing ranges, as well as depth and current conditions. They estimate that a 5-km zone around existing sites makes in excess of 24 000 km2 unavailable for new sites; smaller distance zones would constrain less area. Mattilsynet’s recommendations on minimum distances and coordinated fallowing groups also influence whether sites can be established or expanded. The authors suggest that differentiated, site-sensitive environmental regulation could concentrate production at more suitable locations, potentially increasing output while releasing other areas. They caution that reduced impacts from new technology do not automatically make additional coastal areas available because competing uses and site suitability remain constraints.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify site availability, suitable depth and currents, environmental conditions, fish health, and competing coastal uses as interacting constraints on development. Production is currently limited chiefly by sea-lice conditions and access to suitable aquaculture areas; feed resources may become a future constraint. Total production is governed by concession-MTB under the traffic-light system, while actual use of that capacity also depends on site-MTB and access to cleared, suitable localities. Recommended separation distances and coordinated fallowing arrangements affect both new applications and expansions. Closed or semi-closed systems may reduce sea-lice and disease pressures and permit use of some shallower, calmer or previously unsuitable sites, but they do not remove constraints from effluent, receiving-water capacity, competing uses or high investment costs. The authors stress that growth potential cannot be reliably quantified because uncertainties remain substantial.
pq_notes.A3: The authors argue that more systematic, standardized collection of operational and environmental data from more coastal sites could support research into causal relationships and inform prevention of escapes, understanding of sea lice, technology development and fish welfare. They also identify potential value in nationally collecting and analysing fish-health examination data. Data quality assurance is essential before such evidence is used for conclusions or decisions. Aquacloud is described as developing open-standard protocols for sensor, environmental and fish-health data, while real-time data could support assessments of carrying capacity and environmental pressure in fjord systems during operations and when considering expansions. The segment does not describe a formal cumulative-effects assessment method or how such assessments currently enter planning and site selection; it instead identifies data-sharing and knowledge needs that could support those assessments.
pq_notes.A5: The segment identifies company-collected operational, environmental and fish-health information, public datasets, certification indicators and sustainability KPIs as potential inputs to public management. The authors say that effective use requires high data quality, substantial work to collect and process information, shared terminology, interoperable systems and safeguards for data owners’ rights. BarentsWatch provides an existing public data-sharing platform, and Aquacloud is an industry initiative developing protocols and open standards for sensor, environmental and fish-health data. Standardized data from more sites could support causal research and early warnings for sea-lice or algal blooms and critical weather. The authors also discuss new production concepts and species, whose impacts depend on biology, technology and location; knowledge is limited for concepts still being tested. They caution that the project did not undertake an exhaustive assessment of data potential or quantify growth potential.
pq_notes.A6: The authors describe conflicts between aquaculture development and other coastal interests, including fisheries, tourism, transport, conservation and military areas. Distance recommendations, fallowing coordination and disease risks can also constrain where sites may be established or expanded. The segment does not report particular disputes or application-stage conflicts, but explains that coordinated fallowing is intended to improve fish health and welfare and affects local availability of space. The authors say decision-making on new species needs suitable knowledge and rules adapted to their biology and production methods; otherwise, businesses may have reduced opportunities to develop new industries. They also argue that transparent, quality-assured and shared data, with clear terminology and protection of data-owner rights, would support better-informed and more legitimate management decisions.
pq_notes.A7: The authors point to several actions companies can take: share operational, environmental and fish-health data; collaborate with other operators in the same fjord system; adopt common data protocols; use digital systems and APIs to make information more accessible; and apply private certification schemes, sustainability indicators and KPIs. Some certification standards address parameters not currently requested in Norwegian aquaculture management, such as plastic, or are described as exceeding legal requirements, for example on copper in ASC. The authors suggest that public authorities could examine certification standards and company KPIs to identify whether regulation should be strengthened or new factors included. The text emphasizes that data-sharing initiatives depend on reliable data, common terminology, interoperable systems and respect for data ownership.
pq_notes.A8: The authors describe disease and sea-lice transmission as factors that shape site spacing, fallowing arrangements and production opportunities. Sites in a fallowing area are grouped because nearby farms may affect each other’s receiving environment through the spread of lice and disease. Mattilsynet’s recommended 5 km distance for new grow-out sites outside coordinated fallowing groups is intended to account for these risks, while coordinated operations can affect the distance rules applied. Offshore sites, because of their greater separation from other farms, are expected to be less exposed to infection and less likely to contribute to transmission; the cited examples had low or normal disease frequency, but the authors note that there are few cases. Closed systems may reduce disease and lice risks, but the authors say further investigation is needed to assess disease impacts and receiving-water conditions. The segment also notes a research institute’s concern about potential lice transmission from large offshore farms.

segments.summary:
The segment first considers whether company-collected information can support public management. The authors identify opportunities in standardized operational, environmental and fish-health data, shared data protocols, digitalization and real-time information. BarentsWatch involves 29 administrative agencies and research institutions, while Aquacloud is developing open standards for sensor, environmental and fish-health data. The authors emphasize the need for reliable data, interoperability, shared terminology and protection of data ownership. Company certifications and KPIs may also reveal sustainability issues that current regulation does not cover.

The discussion then turns to new species and production systems. A 2019 assessment considered 30 candidate species, and the authors explain that existing rules developed for salmon may not fit other species. Low-trophic species may use nutrients or particles, while species such as cod can create risks through feed-related emissions and genetic interaction with wild populations. Closed and semi-closed systems may reduce some impacts and allow sites in shallower, calmer waters, but evidence on performance remains limited. At Hamnsundet, Akvafuture recovered 75 tonnes of dry sludge solids from 3319 tonnes of dry feed solids in 2019; the authors estimate the captured share of produced sludge at 6-7 % and caution against unverified claims of high recovery.

The authors describe space, site suitability and fish health as constraints on growth. A recommended 5-km distance around sites makes in excess of 24 000 km2 unavailable for new sites, and just over 65% of current sites were in defined fallowing areas. Growth scenarios are illustrative rather than predictive. The segment also reports that average growth after the traffic-light system’s introduction was 2,9 %, and that growth varied substantially between regions. The authors acknowledge major uncertainties in estimating future growth and impacts.

pq_notes.A0: The authors argue that improved environmental knowledge, data, indicators and analytical methods could enable more precise regulation and more efficient use of the best sites. Their illustrative scenarios show how capacity might be increased at sites with good environmental status and reduced at poorer sites, but they stress that environmental carrying limits must be investigated. Better marine base maps and dispersion models could make site searches more systematic and inform planning from an early stage. The report also says the appropriate scale depends on the pressure: some impacts may be managed locally, while lice and disease require regional or production-area oversight. Shifting production to better sites would require coordination among municipalities, industry actors and other interests, and the distributional consequences could vary substantially among companies.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify site availability and capacity, environmental status, carrying capacity, disease and lice risks, and the fit between licence-MTB and site-MTB as factors shaping development opportunities. Their illustrative B-survey scenarios suggest substantial potential capacity at sites rated Very good, while emphasizing that the survey data are a snapshot and do not account for changes over time. Companies report needing site biomass of approximately 4 times licensed biomass to use licences well; the authors find a positive relationship between site biomass availability and licence utilization. More available site capacity can also enable longer fallowing and movement of fish during harmful algal blooms or disease outbreaks. Better mapping and modelling could improve site selection, but environmental thresholds and local receiving conditions remain important constraints.
pq_notes.A3: The authors argue that cumulative impacts should be assessed through ecosystem-based planning, including the proposed activity, other farms, other types of interventions and wider pressures such as climate change. They identify major knowledge and methodological challenges: ecosystems and cumulative burdens are difficult to define in space and time; local seabed mapping and data on sensitive habitats are incomplete; and indicators and thresholds for ecosystem components exposed to multiple pressures need development. Water-body information should be combined with current and seabed flow data, local surveys and information about other sources such as wastewater. The authors discuss GIS-based cumulative impact assessment models and Strategic Environmental Assessment as potential planning tools, while noting the need for better data, standardized approaches and usable decision support.
pq_notes.A4: The authors define economic efficiency as achieving the greatest combined benefit for a given cost, or a given benefit at the lowest cost. They argue that more locally tailored regulation may reduce environmental risks without unnecessarily limiting production, but that data collection, analysis and administrative costs must be compared with the benefits. Who pays for additional knowledge is identified as a distributional question. The report notes that lice control can impose substantial direct and indirect costs and questions whether traffic-light adjustments have empirically demonstrated environmental effects. It also says the costs of ecosystem-based management should be considered across actors and sectors. Site capacity can support both efficiency and sustainability by allowing fallowing and operational flexibility.
pq_notes.A5: The report identifies B-survey results, environmental monitoring, marine base maps, seabed and habitat data, flow and dispersion models, and information on stressor thresholds as relevant to spatial decisions. It says existing knowledge is often used in management, but could be applied more directly and systematically, including in municipal coastal planning and site searches. Industry-held survey findings could form a valuable shared dataset, but the authors say there is no known system for reporting all such findings, including discoveries of corals or other natural values. They recommend standardized habitat classification, predictive habitat models, combined datasets and GIS or strategic assessment tools. Limitations include weak knowledge of some habitats and stressors, variable data and the need to connect indicators to management actions.
pq_notes.A6: The authors describe potential conflicts over moving production from poorer to better sites, since effects and opportunities may fall unevenly among operators and larger companies may have greater flexibility. Coordination is needed among municipalities, industry actors and other interested parties. The report also cites industry concerns that some county-level authorities impose especially strict sensitive-habitat survey requirements despite a lack of standardized methods, creating different competitive conditions across counties. More broadly, cited work identifies fragmented sectoral administration, policy and power relationships as obstacles to ecosystem-based management. The authors recommend clearer regional guidance and coordination between sectoral requirements, water management and coastal planning to improve consistency and legitimacy.
pq_notes.A7: The authors identify several actions industry can take to support more efficient and sustainable area use: strategically relocate capacity from more disease-spreading sites to less-spreading sites; coordinate operations and production plans; use existing environmental data and models more systematically; and report survey findings and new discoveries of natural values in a systematic way. Capacity at environmentally good sites could be increased where carrying conditions allow, while capacity at poorer sites could be reduced. More site-MTB can also provide room for longer fallowing and for moving fish during algal blooms or disease outbreaks. The report cautions that relocation and capacity changes require investigation of local environmental limits and better coordination among companies and public authorities.
pq_notes.A8: The segment treats water connectivity and site configuration as important to disease and lice transmission. A cited 2020 analysis for production area 3 found that strategic relocation from more disease-spreading to less-spreading sites would likely reduce infection pressure without lowering total capacity; one modelled scenario indicated reductions in transmission between sites of 46% for salmon lice and 30% for viruses when moving from 135 to 100 grow-out sites. The authors say hydrodynamic and dispersion models could help evaluate disease-spread risk, and that preventive coordination between operators is currently encouraged by the Food Safety Authority but is voluntary. They also note that disease can spread across larger areas and therefore requires regional monitoring and management.

segments.summary:
This segment presents a scenario for environmentally guided growth and then discusses how better knowledge could improve aquaculture management and ecosystem-based planning. The authors use B-survey environmental-status results, as of 03.02.23, to illustrate possible changes in site-MTB. Their scenarios suggest that a 6 % increase at sites rated Very good could add just over 130.000 tonnes; including Good-status sites could raise total site-MTB by about 170.000 tonnes. A 6% cut at Poor and Very poor sites would affect just over 17.000 tonnes. They stress that these are illustrative snapshots, not forecasts, and that local carrying capacity must be assessed. A cited production-area 3 analysis found that relocating capacity among 135 and 100 grow-out sites could reduce transmission between sites by 46% for salmon lice and 30% for viruses without reducing total production.

The discussion groups environmental pressures by the strength of evidence and coverage in current regulation, and identifies opportunities for more localized, targeted and economically efficient management. The authors recommend combining marine base maps, flow and dispersion models, environmental thresholds and systematic industry data to improve site selection and assess cumulative pressures. They discuss the costs and uncertain effectiveness of lice regulation, the relationship between licence-MTB and site-MTB, and the value of capacity flexibility for fallowing and responding to disease or algal blooms. For ecosystem-based management, they highlight gaps in habitat mapping, indicators, cumulative-impact methods and cross-sector coordination. GIS-based assessment and Strategic Environmental Assessment are presented as possible planning tools. The authors note that the project was time-limited and did not provide an exhaustive evaluation of ecosystem-based management.

key_figures.statement: A cited study of production area PO3 concluded that the number of grow-out sites could be reduced from 135 to 100 without reducing total production.

key_figures.quote: vi pekte på at en 50 % økning for lokaliteter med Meget god miljøstatus (det gjelder omtrent 2/3 av lokalitetene) vil gi 1,1 millioner tonn økt lokalitets-MTB.
key_figures.statement: The authors estimate that increasing production by 50 % at sites with Very good environmental status, which comprise approximately 2/3 of sites, would add 1,1 million tonnes of site-specific maximum permitted biomass capacity.

pq_notes.A0: The authors argue that growth opportunities depend on regional differences in sea-lice pressure, site suitability, and environmental status. Where lice do not constrain growth, other stressors may become limiting. They emphasize that environmental thresholds and the acceptable level of seabed impact will shape how much production can be allowed, and that decisions will still require trade-offs even with better knowledge. Their scenarios illustrate possible regional redistribution of production and environmentally differentiated growth. They suggest that better use of suitable sites in low-louse areas could support growth while production is constrained elsewhere.
pq_notes.A1: The segment identifies sea lice as the main current constraint on production growth, with effects varying among regions. Site availability and site quality also matter: a lack of new, good sites, combined with limits on site-specific maximum permitted biomass, can constrain growth even where organic emissions are not assessed as production-limiting. Disease is described as a reason for separation requirements that limit use of available areas. The authors discuss whether coordinated operating plans could support more targeted or reduced separation requirements, but present this as a question for future knowledge and management, not an established change.
pq_notes.A3: The segment does not describe a formal cumulative-effects assessment process. It does discuss growth managed according to environmental status across measurable parameters beyond sea lice, allowing production to reflect differences in the carrying capacity of sites and water systems. The authors identify important knowledge and judgment challenges: determining acceptable seabed condition, accounting for impacts that are irreversible or slow to diminish, and deciding what level of environmental risk is acceptable. They cite a study of PO3 that found its site structure could be changed from 135 to 100 grow-out sites without reducing total production, illustrating how spatial configuration can affect production opportunities.
pq_notes.A5: The authors say more local management requires knowledge sufficient to identify the stressors limiting growth in different areas. They ask whether the parameters underlying separation requirements are sufficiently understood to justify reducing those requirements. Organic emissions are described as among the best-monitored environmental impacts; the cited Institute of Marine Research risk assessment (Grefsrud et al., 2022) did not identify them as production-limiting in any production area. However, the segment notes that monitoring and environmental-status classifications do not by themselves resolve what level of impact is acceptable, particularly for irreversible or persistent seabed effects.
pq_notes.A6: The segment frames the central conflict as a trade-off between production growth and avoiding unacceptable environmental impacts and risks. Separation requirements are precautionary measures intended to reduce disease spread or other environmental effects below critical levels, but they also constrain use of coastal areas. The authors argue that decisions will continue to require balancing competing considerations even as knowledge improves. They raise questions about whether current separation distances can be applied more selectively, including through coordinated operating plans, but do not report stakeholder disputes or assess procedural legitimacy.
pq_notes.A7: The authors suggest that industry and managers could make spatial use more efficient by producing more at the best-suited sites, particularly sites in areas where sea lice do not limit growth and sites with Very good environmental status. They also point to moving production from poor to good sites and changing site structures as possible approaches. A cited PO3 analysis found that reducing the number of grow-out sites from 135 to 100 need not reduce total production. The authors present increasing production at environmentally good sites as a possibility requiring judgments about acceptable impact, not as a proven universally safe measure.
pq_notes.A8: Disease is not described as a direct capacity limit, but the authors identify it as an important basis for separation requirements intended to prevent disease spread. Current practice uses a main separation threshold of 5 kilometers, which can be reduced to 2,5 when facilities have coordinated operating plans. The authors ask whether better knowledge of the parameters used to set distances could support more targeted use or further reductions. They do not provide specific evidence on water connectivity, transmission pathways between farms, or biosecurity outcomes.

segments.summary:
This section considers what environmentally responsible aquaculture growth could mean when growth constraints and environmental conditions vary between regions and sites. The authors identify sea lice as the main current growth constraint, while noting that other stressors may become limiting where lice are less problematic. Disease is not presented as a direct capacity constraint, but as an important rationale for precautionary separation rules: a main distance of 5 kilometers can be reduced to 2,5 with coordinated operating plans. The authors ask whether better knowledge could support more targeted use of distance requirements.

Organic emissions are among the best-monitored impacts and, according to the cited Grefsrud et al. (2022) assessment, are not production-limiting in any production area. Nevertheless, site-specific biomass limits and a lack of new good sites can constrain growth. The authors discuss whether sites with Very good environmental status could support more production, while emphasizing uncertainty over acceptable seabed impacts, especially where effects are irreversible or slow to recover.

The section presents scenarios rather than new empirical measurements. With sea lice as the only growth regulator and recent growth patterns continuing, production could approach four million tonnes in 2050; about 4 % annual growth would reach 5 million tonnes. A regional scenario based on recent growth rates projects nearly 2/3 of production in North Norway by 2050 and a decline in Vestland’s salmon and trout share from 23 to 10 %. A cited PO3 study found that reducing sites from 135 to 100 need not reduce total production. The authors also estimate that a 50 % increase at sites with Very good status, about 2/3 of sites, would add 1,1 million tonnes of site-specific biomass capacity. These possibilities remain contingent on environmental judgments and management choices.

segments.summary: This segment contains appendices documenting literature search profiles rather than findings about aquaculture siting or area management. Appendix A provides search strategies for aquaculture-related topics including particulate organic waste, dissolved nutrients, environmental contaminants, escapes, disease and parasites, noise, light, and artificial structures. It identifies search dates and, in several cases, the people who conducted the searches. The searches use databases such as Web of Science, Scopus, WorldCat Dissertations and Theses, and ORIA. The search strings combine aquaculture and species terms with stressor and impact terms, and often limit searches to English-language publications from 2010–2022. The segment notes that year restrictions were not applied to some Web of Science and Scopus searches for noise, light, and artificial structures because literature was limited. Appendix B describes search profiles for effects of other industries on aquaculture and supplies Web of Science retrieval counts: 595 records for particles, 424 for dissolved nutrients, 1062 for physical damage, 2183 for contaminants, 52 for noise, 7 for light, 1541 for warming, and 73 for stepping stones (artificial structures). These are search-result counts, not estimates of environmental effects or aquaculture impacts. The segment gives no synthesis of the retrieved studies, no spatial-planning evidence, and no conclusions on cumulative effects, licensing, or site selection. Search-string details and database choices define the scope of the evidence gathering, but the segment does not report screening outcomes or the number of studies ultimately included.

pq_notes.A0: The authors’ review of case documents shows that establishment and expansion are assessed through several sector authorities, with environmental permits, municipal plans, fisheries interests and fish-health rules all affecting outcomes. Statsforvalteren cases invoke pollution law, the Nature Diversity Act and the Water Framework Regulations, and may require monitoring or limit production. County-level decisions often rely on earlier site clearances and sector-authority statements; the review found few explicit balancing methods beyond the allocation regulations in many cases. Some reviewed decisions permit changes despite concerns, while others defer or oppose them because the evidence is insufficient, the receiving environment is deteriorating, or interests such as wild fish and fisheries may be harmed. These are documented cases, not a single uniform decision rule.
pq_notes.A1: The reviewed cases indicate that development opportunities depend on suitable and available locations, applicable plans, environmental capacity, sector-authority assessments and fish-health considerations. Site applications draw on current-area plans, environmental surveys, currents, oxygen, seabed information, mapped biodiversity and fisheries data. Statsforvalteren may require additional coral surveys, recipient monitoring, oxygen measurements or other conditions, and may withhold support until evidence is available. Mattilsynet assesses distances to existing farms and rivers, disease and parasite transmission, production-area boundaries, and effects on wild populations. The case review also shows species-specific differences: cod has a different production cycle from salmon, which can complicate coordinated fallowing, and the cited guidance does not set the same requirements for all species. The tables illustrate interacting constraints rather than a general estimate of available sites.
pq_notes.A2: The segment presents case-document tables rather than a step-by-step account of the application procedure. Applications and changes are assessed by sector authorities, with county authorities making licensing decisions and municipal plans and public consultation appearing in the evidence base. Delays or requests for further information arise where environmental data are missing: in one case, Statsforvalteren said expansion could be reconsidered when recipient-survey results were available. Rejections or recommendations against approval also occur at sector-authority stages. Mattilsynet rejected a land-based salmon application because the distance to existing sites was far below its recommended minimum and the authority could not conclude that disease-spread risk was absent. Other cases show recommendations against establishment because of wild anadromous fish or insufficient knowledge. The segment does not quantify how often delays, rejections or conflicts occur across all applications.
pq_notes.A3: The authors’ case review finds that some decisions explicitly consider total ecosystem load, including uncertainty about whether a recipient or ecosystem can tolerate combined pressures. One Statsforvalteren case notes uncertainty in the available knowledge about effects of nutrient and organic discharges and applies the precautionary principle. Another case permits an expansion on the condition that a different site closes, keeping total maximum allowable biomass unchanged, despite a long-term negative trend in the recipient. However, the tables also show uneven evidence and practice: some applications lack adequate environmental data, and some decisions request recipient surveys or fjord-wide monitoring before firm conclusions. Fisheries Directorate cases cite risk reports and environmental surveys but sometimes note that there is insufficient knowledge about effects on cod spawning areas and no general management advice. The segment documents case-level assessment, not a common cumulative-effects method.
pq_notes.A5: The reviewed decisions use a varied knowledge base: municipal and coastal plans; mapped fisheries and biodiversity; AIS, VMS, tracking and sales-slip data; interviews and consultation; environmental surveys; current and oxygen measurements; seabed mapping; and reports from the Institute of Marine Research and other bodies. The cases reveal gaps and uneven documentation. Several authorities state that knowledge about aquaculture effects on cod spawning grounds is insufficient, and one Statsforvalteren decision says the ecosystem-wide effects of discharges remain uncertain. Tools and data such as current catalogues, risk reports, Naturbase, Vann-nett and ROV surveys inform assessments, but their presence does not always resolve uncertainty. The segment does not discuss emerging technologies as a general driver of siting or environmental change; it gives case examples such as closed systems, partial closure and seabed or coral mapping.
pq_notes.A6: The case review identifies conflicts with commercial and recreational fisheries, traditional fishing grounds, crab and shrimp grounds, spawning areas, wild salmon and trout, corals, protected or sensitive habitats, and other aquaculture operators. Fisheries authorities sometimes recommend limiting mooring lines or adapting plans; in other cases, an application is accepted because the area is zoned for aquaculture or the fishing ground can remain partly usable. Mattilsynet may reject a site where disease risk to neighbouring facilities cannot be ruled out, even if the likelihood is considered small, because consequences could be serious. Legitimate and predictable decisions are supported in the cases by clear evidence, consultation, explicit conditions and reasons, and precaution where uncertainty remains. But the tables also show inconsistent documentation, including decisions with no case presentation or explicit balancing, which can weaken transparency and predictability.
pq_notes.A7: Some reviewed decisions identify operational measures that applicants or operators can use to reduce spatial or environmental impacts. Fisheries authorities recommend limiting the extent of mooring lines and maintaining dialogue with local fishers; one decision specifies that moorings should not be placed in shallow water. A county-level decision gives weight to a feed barge and expanded area because these could reduce feed waste and improve economic and environmental operation. County authorities also encourage minimizing lice-treatment medicines and considering other users. Statsforvalteren conditions include monitoring, mapping sensitive habitats, and, in one case, requiring an alternative site to close so the expansion does not increase total maximum allowable biomass. These examples are case-specific measures, not a comprehensive industry-wide sustainability standard.
pq_notes.A8: Mattilsynet’s reviewed cases treat farm spacing, currents, fallowing coordination, production cycles and proximity to wild populations as relevant to disease and parasite risk. A land-based salmon application was rejected because the proposed location was much closer than recommended to established sites; the authority could not rule out transmission to neighbours despite proposed controls. A reviewed cod-site approval notes that cod’s biology and production cycle differ from salmon’s, so placing a cod farm between salmon farms could undermine coordinated fallowing if pathogens cross species. Other cases assess lice reports, treatments, currents and distances to nearby farms and rivers. The tables also distinguish parasite host ranges: the cited assessment says salmon lice primarily use salmonids, while sea lice can infect multiple fish species. Cod decisions discuss disease transmission to wild cod and use distance and current modelling, while acknowledging uncertainty. These are case-specific regulatory assessments, not a general quantitative model of water connectivity.

This appendix presents the authors’ review of case documents from aquaculture authorities, organized by Statsforvalteren, the Fisheries Directorate, Mattilsynet and county municipalities. It records application types, legal bases, information used, assessments and monitoring conditions. The cases show that environmental decisions draw on recipient surveys, current and oxygen measurements, seabed and coral mapping, biodiversity records, fisheries data, coastal plans and risk reports. Authorities commonly identify uncertainty about ecosystem-level effects, discharges, wild fish and cod spawning areas. Responses include precautionary conditions, additional surveys and monitoring, limits on production or moorings, and—in some cases—recommendations against or rejection of applications.

The case examples also illustrate interaction between spatial use and biosecurity. Mattilsynet considers farm distances, disease transmission, lice pressure, rivers, production-area boundaries and coordination of fallowing. One reviewed land-based salmon application was rejected on disease-risk grounds, while the cases include recommended distances of 2,5 km to other food-fish sites and 5 km to broodstock sites for cod. Fisheries cases document conflicts with fishing grounds, gear, crab and shrimp fisheries, and spawning areas; some decisions seek coexistence through conditions or adjustments. A reviewed permit allowed trout broodstock production of 1560 tonn MTB for six years, while another case describes 50 km as an acceptable distance from national salmon rivers and fjords.

The appendix is a descriptive compilation of selected case documents, not a statistical assessment of all applications. It reveals variation in evidence, reasoning and documentation, including cases with missing or limited explanations. It does not establish how frequently each outcome occurs or provide a common method for cumulative-effect assessment.
